title: As an ops user, I can build multi-step workflows in a visual editor without writing code
As an ops user, I can branch a workflow with conditions, filters, and parallel paths that merge back together
As a developer, I can compose reusable sub-workflows or modules that other workflows call
As a developer, I can test a workflow with sample or pinned data and inspect each step's input and output before going live
As an ops user, I can trigger workflows from events in connected apps (new record, message, email, form submission)
As an ops user, I can run workflows on cron-style schedules with timezone control
As a developer, I can expose a custom webhook URL that receives external HTTP requests and starts a workflow run with the payload
As a developer, I can configure automatic retries with backoff for failed steps or activities
As an ops user, I can define dedicated error-handling paths or error workflows and get notified when a run fails
As an ops user, I can inspect past execution logs and re-run a failed execution, resuming from the failing step
As a developer, I can run long-lived workflows that wait for days and survive worker or platform restarts without losing state
As a developer, I can throttle or queue workflow executions to respect downstream rate limits
As a developer, I can drop into real code (JavaScript or Python) as a step inside a workflow
As a developer, I can build a custom connector or private integration with a documented developer platform, SDK, or CLI
As an ops user, I can map and transform data between steps with expressions, functions, or formulas
As an ops user, I can connect to thousands of apps through prebuilt, vendor-maintained integrations
As an ops user, I can start from a public library of workflow templates instead of building from scratch
As a developer, I can install community-built nodes, components, or integrations contributed outside the vendor
As an ops user, I can store connection credentials centrally, share them with my team, and control who can use which credential
As a developer, I can version workflows through source control or environments and promote changes from dev to production
As an ops user, I can pause a workflow to wait for human approval or input before it continues
As a developer, I can run workflows locally or against a dev instance for development and CI testing
As a developer, I can embed the automation platform white-label inside my own product for my customers
As an AI-native user, I can add AI agent or LLM steps inside a workflow, with model choice and tool use
As an AI-native user, I can generate or edit a workflow from a natural-language prompt
As an AI-native user, I can expose my workflows or connected app actions as MCP tools that an external agent can call
As an AI-native user, I can have an agent create, update, and activate a workflow programmatically through the public API
